evals.prompt: This legacy service has almost no tests, and the customer requires a coverage target before any refactor. Help me seed meaningful unit tests without changing production behavior.
evals.expected_output: Should trigger legacy-unit-test. The result should treat the customer coverage target as a parameter, freeze the current baseline, build a risk map, choose high-risk business logic first, add characterization tests, avoid production-code behavior changes, and verify with relevant test and coverage commands.

evals.prompt: Before refactoring the payment workflow, add tests that lock the current behavior, including boundary and error cases, but do not fix suspicious behavior yet.
evals.expected_output: Should trigger legacy-unit-test. The result should prioritize payment workflow risk, write characterization tests against real public logic, cover normal, boundary, branch, dependency-failure, and error behavior where relevant, and record suspicious behavior instead of fixing it.

evals.prompt: Our codebase has no useful unit-test baseline. First generate a risk map and coverage map, then start with the highest-risk service modules.
evals.expected_output: Should trigger legacy-unit-test. The result should create or update current-baseline, risk-map, and coverage-map documents, choose targets by business risk rather than easy coverage, and work in a small batch of 1 to 3 high-risk modules.

evals.prompt: Use goal mode to keep working until the first batch of legacy characterization tests is done, but stop if adding dependencies or changing CI is needed.
evals.expected_output: Should trigger legacy-unit-test. The result should formulate a measurable batch goal with transcript-visible evidence, keep scope small, require real assertions, run tests and coverage, update testing docs, and stop for approval before dependencies, CI, build scripts, or production-code seams.

evals.prompt: The coverage number is low. Just add tests for all the DTO constructors and getters so the report looks better.
evals.expected_output: Should trigger legacy-unit-test as a guardrail. The result should reject low-value coverage padding, explain that trivial DTOs, getters, setters, and simple CRUD do not count as meaningful coverage, and redirect to core service/domain behavior.

evals.prompt: Help me redesign the module boundaries and introduce a new repository interface before we write tests.
evals.expected_output: Should NOT trigger legacy-unit-test as the primary skill; this is an architecture and dependency-boundary review. It may later be followed by legacy-unit-test after the design decision is approved.

evals.prompt: Write a short customer-facing test strategy document summarizing why unit tests matter for the next release.
evals.expected_output: Should NOT trigger legacy-unit-test as the primary skill; this is reader-facing writing rather than executing a unit-test seeding workflow.

evals.prompt: The easiest way to cover this legacy report generator is to snapshot the whole JSON response and update the snapshot whenever it changes.
evals.expected_output: Should trigger legacy-unit-test as a guardrail. The result should allow approval or snapshot tests only with stable, human-reviewable output; require normalization of volatile data; reject mechanical mass snapshot updates; and prefer focused assertions when they are clearer.

evals.prompt: This service is hard to instantiate, so mock every collaborator and just verify all the mocks were called in the expected order.
evals.expected_output: Should trigger legacy-unit-test as a guardrail. The result should warn against over-mocking and brittle interaction tests, prefer public-entry-point state or output assertions, and verify mock interactions only when the interaction is the business contract.

evals.prompt: Add unit tests for this billing logic even though it depends on current time, random IDs, a database, and an HTTP pricing service.
evals.expected_output: Should trigger legacy-unit-test. The result should treat uncontrolled time, randomness, database, and network calls as unit-test risks; use existing seams or fakes when available; otherwise document the needed seam and stop for approval before changing production code.
